title: Less friction
hook: small bits of effort shape behavior more than willpower

segments.voice: Yesterday's line was the place holds it: a habit is tied to its setting, so a chosen spot can help it last.

A cafeteria line, lunchtime, trays sliding along a rail. Researchers quietly move one dish a little farther back, just beyond easy reach. Nobody hides it. Nobody makes a rule. Anyone who wants it only has to lean in. And people take less of it. Not because they made a resolution, or summoned some inner strength. Because of a lean. Habit researchers draw a strange lesson from studies like this one: the tiniest bit of extra effort, a step, a reach, a second click, can move behavior more than all the willpower anyone brought to lunch.
screen: `A DISH, A LITTLE FARTHER BACK.` → `NOBODY MAKES A RULE.` → `PEOPLE TAKE LESS.`

segments.voice: First, the reach. In cafeteria studies, researchers led by Paul Rozin found that making a food slightly harder to get to, a little farther away, reduced how much of it people took. A small change in distance, a real change in behavior. Second, friction beats will, or so habit researchers argue. Psychologists who study habit, Wendy Wood among them, call these small costs friction. Willpower is what people tend to reach for first, and it can be unreliable. Friction works quietly, without asking anyone to try harder. Third, add friction to what you'd rather do less: the phone charging in another room, the snacks on a high shelf. Not a ban, just a small hill to climb, and small hills turn out to matter. Fourth, take friction away from what you want to do more: the running shoes by the door, the cushion already on the floor, the book on the pillow instead of the shelf. William James, in his chapter on habit, wrote: "The great thing, then, in all education, is to make our nervous system our ally instead of our enemy." Friction is one of the plainest ways to do that: rearrange the room so the easy thing and the good thing are the same thing. A practice that needs a heroic effort to begin may not survive a busy week. A practice that's one step away has a fighting chance.
screen: `A LITTLE FARTHER AWAY.` · `FRICTION BEATS WILL.` · `A SMALL HILL FOR WHAT YOU WANT LESS.` · then, large: `ALLY INSTEAD OF ENEMY.`

segments.voice: Settle on the breath, then walk through tomorrow's practice step by step, the way it actually happens, and find the one step that most often stops you. Picture removing it, the cushion left out, the app moved to the first screen, the alarm set the night before, and choose just one. Then let the planning go and rest on the breath.
Less friction. Small bits of effort shape what people do more than willpower, so make the good thing one step easier. Today's word.
Your line: less friction. A small hill can matter more than a big push. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: People building a habit sometimes arrange their surroundings so the practice takes as few steps as possible, leaving out what they need the night before, and put small obstacles in the way of habits they want to do less.
